question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

Do you have the faint / idea of what would happen / if Maa sees this?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Do you have the faint.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed English collocation is "the faintest idea" — the superlative degree is compulsory in this negative/interrogative expression meaning "the slightest notion". (ज़रा भी अंदाज़ा)

◦ "Faint" as a plain adjective means dim or weak; with "idea" in this idiom only the superlative form faintest is used.

◦ Correct: Do you have the faintest idea of what would happen if Maa sees this?

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 3 "if Maa sees this?" is correct — a present simple in the if-clause of a first conditional is standard.

• Option 4 "idea of what would happen" is correct — "idea of" + noun clause is a proper structure.

• Option 1 is wrong because the sentence does contain an error in the first segment.

NOTE

• Similar superlative-only idioms: not the slightest doubt, not the remotest chance, the least bit, not the foggiest idea.

• "Faintest" also appears in "I haven't the faintest idea" — a very common SSC error-spotting item.

question:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.

Leaders are self-direct, / but learning and understanding / are the keys to self-direction.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Leaders are self-direct,.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• After the linking verb are, a subject complement is required — an adjective, not a verb. "Self-direct" is a verb form; the adjective is self-directed. (स्व-निर्देशित)

◦ Structure: Subject + be + adjective/past participle used adjectivally.

◦ Correct: Leaders are self-directed, but learning and understanding are the keys to self-direction.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "but learning and understanding" is correct — two gerunds joined by "and" form a compound subject.

• Option 4 "are the keys to self-direction." is correct — the plural verb "are" agrees with the compound plural subject.

• Option 1 is wrong because the sentence does contain an error.

NOTE

• Verb → adjective (-ed) pairs often tested: motivate → motivated, dedicate → dedicated, experience → experienced, skill → skilled.

• Remember: "He is interested in music" (not "He is interest in music").

question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.

I smiled at my son and ______ thankful.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. felt.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Two verbs joined by "and" must be parallel in tense. "Smiled" is past simple, so the second verb must also be past simple — felt. (समानांतरता / Parallelism)

◦ "Feel" is an irregular verb: feel – felt – felt.

◦ Correct: I smiled at my son and felt thankful.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "feeling" is a participle and breaks the parallel structure after "and".

• Option 3 "fallen" is a past participle, needs an auxiliary, and gives no sense with "thankful".

• Option 4 "feel" is present tense and clashes with the past tense "smiled".

NOTE

• Parallelism rule: verbs joined by and / or / but share the same form — "She opened the door and walked in."

• "Feel" is a linking verb here, so it takes an adjective (thankful), not an adverb.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

Reservation
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Openness.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Reservation here means a doubt, hesitation or holding back of one's true feelings. (आपत्ति / झिझक)

◦ Openness means frankness, candour, being free from reserve — the exact opposite of holding back.

◦ Correct: He accepted the offer with openness, not with reservation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Catch — to seize or grasp something (पकड़ना); unrelated to reservation.

• Conserve — to protect or save from loss (संरक्षित करना); a near-synonym of "reserve", not an antonym.

• Doubt — uncertainty (संदेह); this is a synonym of reservation, so it cannot be the antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of reservation: hesitation, misgiving, qualm, scepticism, proviso.

• Synonyms of openness: candour, frankness, transparency, receptiveness.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym to substitute the bracketed word in the given sentence.

I do not object to this (accolade) on the grounds that Edinburgh has little literary tradition.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Praise.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Accolade means an award, honour or expression of praise publicly given. (प्रशंसा / सम्मान)

◦ The sentence speaks of an honour conferred on Edinburgh, so a positive word is needed.

◦ Correct: I do not object to this praise on the grounds that Edinburgh has little literary tradition.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Stubborn — obstinate, refusing to change (ज़िद्दी); an adjective, so it cannot replace a noun.

• Criticism — disapproval or fault-finding (आलोचना); the opposite of accolade.

• Indictment — a formal charge or accusation (अभियोग); strongly negative.

NOTE

• Synonyms of accolade: tribute, commendation, honour, kudos, plaudit, laurels.

• Antonyms of accolade: censure, condemnation, rebuke, reproach.

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
option_1: Such blooms typiclly don't lead to deaths.
option_2: Such blooms typically don't leade to deaths.
option_3: Such blooms typically don't lead to deaths.
option_4: Such bloms typically don't lead to deaths.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Such blooms typically don't lead to deaths.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Every word in Option 3 is spelt correctly: blooms, typically, lead, deaths.

◦ Typically = typical + ly; the base word ends in -al, so the adverb keeps double "l". (आमतौर पर)

◦ Correct: Such blooms typically don't lead to deaths.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 misspells "typically" as typiclly (the "a" is missing).

• Option 2 misspells "lead" as leade (extra final "e").

• Option 4 misspells "blooms" as bloms (missing "o").

NOTE

• Adjective + -ly adverbs frequently misspelt: basically, practically, specifically, occasionally, accidentally.

• Note the pair lead (to guide, verb) vs led (its past form) vs lead (the metal, pronounced "led").

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

Converge
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Coincide.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Converge means to come together and meet at a common point. (एक बिंदु पर मिलना)

◦ Coincide means to occupy the same place or to happen at the same time — i.e. to come together; hence it is the closest synonym.

◦ Correct: The two roads converge (= coincide) near the bridge.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Homicide — the killing of one human being by another (हत्या).

• Verbicide — the deliberate distortion or destruction of the sense of a word.

• Fratricide — the killing of one's own brother (भ्रातृहत्या).

NOTE

• Antonym of converge: diverge, separate, scatter, disperse.

• The suffix -cide means "killing": patricide (father), matricide (mother), regicide (king), suicide (self), infanticide (infant), genocide (a race).

question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. Select the option 'no correction required' if the sentence is correct as given.

(Most time) they didn't have enough to eat and went to bed hungry
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Many a time.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Many a is always followed by a singular noun — "many a time", "many a man", "many a day". The adverbial phrase many a time means "often / on many occasions". (अक्सर)

◦ The sentence needs an adverbial of frequency, and "many a time" fits the past-tense narration perfectly.

◦ Correct: Many a time they didn't have enough to eat and went to bed hungry.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is wrong because "Most time" is ungrammatical here; "most of the time" would be needed.

• Option 2 "Many a times" is wrong — "many a" can never take a plural noun.

• Option 3 "More times" is incomplete; comparatives need "than" or a defining phrase.

NOTE

• Many a + singular noun + singular verb: "Many a student has failed."

• Compare: A great many + plural noun + plural verb: "A great many students have failed."

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Contaxte.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is Context — the setting or circumstances surrounding an event or word. (संदर्भ)

◦ "Contaxte" wrongly inserts an "a" and adds a silent "e"; there is no such English word.

◦ Correct: The word must be understood in its proper context.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Station — a stopping place or a post (स्टेशन); correctly spelt.

• Magic — the art of producing illusions (जादू); correctly spelt.

• Charity — help given to those in need (दान); correctly spelt.

NOTE

• Related family: context, contextual, contextualise, pretext, texture — all from Latin *texere* (to weave).

• Frequently misspelt SSC words: occurrence, maintenance, privilege, committee, embarrass, conscience.

question:
Select the appropriate antonym for the underlined word.

What youthful philosophers and experimentalists we are!
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. ripened.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Youthful means young, immature, inexperienced or fresh. (युवा / अपरिपक्व)

◦ Ripened means fully matured or developed — the direct opposite of youthful/immature.

◦ Correct: They are not youthful but ripened philosophers.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Unformed — not fully developed or shaped; a synonym of youthful/immature, not an antonym.

• Childlike — having the innocence of a child; again close in sense to youthful.

• Raw — inexperienced, untrained (कच्चा / अनुभवहीन); also a synonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of youthful: juvenile, adolescent, boyish, girlish, callow, green.

• Antonyms of youthful: mature, aged, seasoned, veteran, elderly, ripe.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.

Diseases passed from animals to humans are called zoonoses.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence is grammatically complete and correct as printed. Diseases is the plural subject and are called is the matching plural passive verb. (कर्मवाच्य)

◦ "passed from animals to humans" is a reduced relative clause (= which are passed from animals to humans) correctly using the past participle passed.

◦ Correct: Diseases passed from animals to humans are called zoonoses.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Diseases passed from" is correct — participle modifiers follow the noun they describe.

• Option 3 "animals to humans" is correct — the pair from ... to ... is properly completed.

• Option 2 "are called zoonoses." is correct — the passive of the object-complement verb "call".

NOTE

• Reduced relative clauses: "The book written by him" = "The book which was written by him".

• Zoonoses (singular: zoonosis) are diseases transmitted from animals to humans — e.g. rabies, plague, anthrax.

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

I think she's right to warn you not to ______ your temper.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. lose.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed idiom is "lose one's temper", meaning to become suddenly angry. (आपा खोना)

◦ No other verb collocates with "temper" in this sense; "keep one's temper" is its opposite.

◦ Correct: I think she's right to warn you not to lose your temper.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "drop your temper" is not an English collocation.

• Option 2 "last" is intransitive here (to continue) and cannot take "your temper" as an object.

• Option 4 "forget your temper" is meaningless; one forgets facts, names or events, not a temper.

NOTE

• Related idioms: lose heart (become discouraged), lose face (be humiliated), lose track of, lose one's cool.

• Do not confuse lose (verb, to misplace) with loose (adjective, not tight).

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.

He had thrown the wrapper into the garbage.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. No improvement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• had thrown is the correct past perfect form: had + V3 (past participle). The verb throw is irregular: throw – threw – thrown. (पूर्ण भूतकाल)

◦ The past perfect suits an action completed before another past point or before the present narration.

◦ Correct: He had thrown the wrapper into the garbage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "throw the" leaves the sentence without the required past-perfect auxiliary structure.

• Option 2 "thrown the" gives a bare past participle with no auxiliary — ungrammatical.

• Option 4 "has throwing the" is doubly wrong: "has" needs V3, not V-ing, and the tense shifts illogically.

NOTE

• Perfect tenses always use have/has/had + V3: "She has written", "They had gone".

• Common V1–V2–V3 traps: throw–threw–thrown, fly–flew–flown, draw–drew–drawn, grow–grew–grown.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.

A place for housing aeroplanes
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Hangar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A hangar is a large shed or building in which aircraft are kept and serviced. (विमानशाला)

◦ It is the standard one-word substitution for "a place for housing aeroplanes".

◦ Correct: The damaged aircraft was towed into the hangar for repairs.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Hutch — a box or cage for keeping rabbits or other small animals.

• Brewery — a place where beer is manufactured (शराब कारख़ाना).

• Burrow — a hole or tunnel dug in the ground by a small animal such as a rabbit.

NOTE

• Do not confuse hangar (aircraft shed) with hanger (a device for hanging clothes).

• Other place words: aviary (birds), apiary (bees), granary (grain), arsenal (weapons), dairy (milk), aquarium (fish).

question:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate option.

As he walked past the chambers, Samir asked everyone to quiet ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. down.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Quiet down is a phrasal verb meaning to become less noisy or to calm down. (शांत हो जाना)

◦ The context — walking past the chambers and asking everyone to stop making noise — demands exactly this sense.

◦ Correct: As he walked past the chambers, Samir asked everyone to quiet down.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "quiet please" cannot follow "to" in an infinitive; the structure "asked everyone to quiet please" is ungrammatical.

• Option 2 "quiet rise" is not an English combination and gives no meaning.

• Option 3 "quiet up" is not a standard phrasal verb; the particle for reducing noise is down, not "up".

NOTE

• Similar "down" phrasal verbs of reduction: calm down, settle down, slow down, cool down, tone down.

• Contrast with "up" verbs of increase: speak up, hurry up, liven up.

question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. Select the option 'no correction required' if the sentence is correct as given.

(Many man) have tried to find the caves but none have succeeded.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Many a man.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct structure is many a + singular countable noun, meaning "a great number of". (अनेक)

◦ "Many man" is ungrammatical; the determiner "many" alone must take a plural noun (many men), while "many a" takes the singular (many a man).

◦ Correct: Many a man has tried to find the caves but none have succeeded.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Much man" is wrong — much is used with uncountable nouns (much water, much time).

• Option 2 is wrong because the printed segment "Many man" is grammatically defective.

• Option 4 "Many a men" is wrong — "many a" can never be followed by a plural noun.

NOTE

• Grammatically "many a man" takes a singular verb: "Many a man has come."

• Countability: many/few/number of + plural countable; much/little/amount of + uncountable.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The life of the church seems, indeed, to have been in a more stagnant and ______ condition in this age than at any other period of English history.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. torpid.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Torpid means sluggish, inactive, lacking energy or motion. (सुस्त / निष्क्रिय)

◦ The blank is joined by "and" to stagnant, so a word of similar negative, inactive sense is required — torpid fits exactly.

◦ Correct: The life of the church seems to have been in a more stagnant and torpid condition in this age.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Tangential — only slightly relevant, going off at a tangent; does not describe a condition of inactivity.

• Expedite — a verb meaning to speed up a process; a verb cannot fill an adjective slot before "condition".

• Truculent — aggressive, quarrelsome and defiant; the opposite in tone to "stagnant".

NOTE

• Synonyms of torpid: lethargic, dormant, listless, inert, languid.

• Antonyms of torpid: active, energetic, vigorous, brisk, lively.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.

To strain every nerve
option_2: To manipulate someone in the best way
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To make a great effort.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to strain every nerve" means to try one's utmost, to exert oneself to the maximum. (एड़ी-चोटी का ज़ोर लगाना)

◦ It is figurative; the literal picture of tightening every nerve conveys total effort.

◦ Correct: He strained every nerve to complete the project before the deadline.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 takes the word "nerve" literally as a medical term — idioms are never literal.

• Option 2 "to manipulate someone" refers to controlling others, not to self-exertion.

• Option 3 "to claim something" means to demand as a right; unrelated to effort.

NOTE

• Similar idioms: to leave no stone unturned, to move heaven and earth, to go all out, to bend over backwards.

• Other "nerve" idioms: to lose one's nerve (lose courage), to have the nerve (to be bold/impudent), to get on someone's nerves (to irritate).

question:
Select the most appropriate word for the given group of words.

To reveal a secret
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Divulge.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Divulge means to make known private or sensitive information; to reveal a secret. (भेद खोलना)

◦ It is the exact one-word substitution for the given group of words.

◦ Correct: He refused to divulge the details of the agreement.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Vilify — to speak or write about someone in an abusively disparaging manner (बदनाम करना).

• Conceal — to hide or keep something secret; the opposite of divulge.

• Discern — to perceive or recognise something with difficulty (समझ लेना).

NOTE

• Synonyms of divulge: disclose, reveal, unveil, impart, let slip, betray.

• Antonyms of divulge: conceal, hide, withhold, suppress, hush up.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Be at a crossroads
option_1: To have taken the wrong road
option_3: To make a very important decision
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To make a very important decision.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "be at a crossroads" means to be at a point where a crucial, life-changing choice has to be made. (निर्णायक मोड़ पर होना)

◦ The image is of standing where roads meet and having to choose which one to take.

◦ Correct: After losing his job, Ravi was at a crossroads in his career.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "to have taken the wrong road" is a literal reading; the idiom is about choosing, not about a mistake already made.

• Option 2 "to be confused" is close but incomplete — the essence of the idiom is the important decision, not mere confusion.

• Option 4 "to have forgotten the way" is again a literal misreading.

NOTE

• Related idioms: at a turning point, at the fork in the road, moment of truth.

• "Crossroads" is used with a singular verb even though it ends in -s: "A crossroads is ahead."

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

Professor Sprout was standing (1) ______ a trestle bench in the centre of the greenhouse. (2) ______ twenty (3) ______ of different-coloured ear muffs (4) ______ lying on the bench. Harry (5) ______ his place between Ron and Hermione.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. behind.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank needs a preposition to link "was standing" with the noun phrase "a trestle bench". Behind = at the back of. (के पीछे)

◦ A teacher demonstrating to a class naturally stands behind the bench, facing the students.

◦ Correct: Professor Sprout was standing behind a trestle bench in the centre of the greenhouse.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "back off" is a phrasal verb meaning to retreat; it cannot join a verb to a noun here.

• Option 2 "after back" is not a valid English expression.

• Option 4 "afterwards" is an adverb of time, not a preposition of place, so it cannot take an object.

NOTE

• Prepositions of place: behind, in front of, beside, between, among, across, beneath.

• Remember: a preposition must always be followed by an object (noun/pronoun/gerund); an adverb never is.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

Professor Sprout was standing (1) ______ a trestle bench in the centre of the greenhouse. (2) ______ twenty (3) ______ of different-coloured ear muffs (4) ______ lying on the bench. Harry (5) ______ his place between Ron and Hermione.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. About.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Before a number, about means "approximately" — "about twenty" = roughly twenty. (लगभग)

◦ The narrator is estimating the number of pairs of ear muffs, so an approximator is required.

◦ Correct: About twenty pairs of different-coloured ear muffs were lying on the bench.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Near by" (nearby) refers to place, not to quantity, and cannot modify a number.

• Option 2 "Utmost" is an adjective meaning greatest/most extreme; it does not express approximation.

• Option 4 "Round" would need "around" in this sense; "Round twenty" is not standard written English here.

NOTE

• Other approximators before numbers: around, nearly, almost, roughly, some, approximately.

• "About" also means "concerning": "a book about birds."

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

Professor Sprout was standing (1) ______ a trestle bench in the centre of the greenhouse. (2) ______ twenty (3) ______ of different-coloured ear muffs (4) ______ lying on the bench. Harry (5) ______ his place between Ron and Hermione.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. pairs.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Objects that consist of two matching items used together are counted in pairs — a pair of ear muffs, shoes, gloves, spectacles, scissors. (जोड़ी)

◦ Ear muffs come as two joined cups, so "pairs of ear muffs" is the only correct collocation.

◦ Correct: About twenty pairs of different-coloured ear muffs were lying on the bench.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "couples" is used mainly for two people in a relationship or for "a couple of" (a few), not for matching objects.

• Option 3 "teams" refers to groups of people or animals working together.

• Option 4 "duality" is an abstract noun meaning the state of having two parts; it cannot be counted with "twenty ... of".

NOTE

• Nouns always plural, counted with "pair of": trousers, scissors, spectacles, pliers, tongs, pyjamas.

• Collective usage: a flock of sheep, a herd of cattle, a swarm of bees, a bunch of keys.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

Professor Sprout was standing (1) ______ a trestle bench in the centre of the greenhouse. (2) ______ twenty (3) ______ of different-coloured ear muffs (4) ______ lying on the bench. Harry (5) ______ his place between Ron and Hermione.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. were.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject is pairs (plural), so the past continuous requires the plural auxiliary were + V-ing (lying). (कर्ता-क्रिया मेल)

◦ Subject–verb agreement is decided by the head noun "pairs", not by the following noun "ear muffs".

◦ Correct: About twenty pairs of different-coloured ear muffs were lying on the bench.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "lay" would give "lay lying", a double verb — ungrammatical.

• Option 2 "was" is singular and does not agree with the plural subject "pairs".

• Option 4 "continue" is present tense and clashes with the past narration, besides not fitting with "lying".

NOTE

• Past continuous: was/were + V-ing, for actions in progress at a past moment.

• Distinguish lie – lay – lain (to recline) from lay – laid – laid (to place something).

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

Professor Sprout was standing (1) ______ a trestle bench in the centre of the greenhouse. (2) ______ twenty (3) ______ of different-coloured ear muffs (4) ______ lying on the bench. Harry (5) ______ his place between Ron and Hermione.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. had taken.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The whole passage is narrated in the past, so a past perfect (had + V3) is needed to show that Harry had already occupied his place. (पूर्ण भूतकाल)

◦ Take is irregular: take – took – taken; "had taken" is the correct past perfect form.

◦ Correct: Harry had taken his place between Ron and Hermione.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "have to take" expresses present obligation and breaks the past narration.

• Option 3 "has took" is doubly wrong — "has" must take V3 "taken", and the tense is present perfect.

• Option 4 "have taken" is present perfect and also disagrees with the singular subject "Harry".

NOTE

• Sequence of tenses: in a past narration, earlier actions take the past perfect.

• Collocation: take one's place / take one's seat = to occupy the position meant for one.
